sections.h2: Which Early County office handles what
sections.html:
The Early County Assessor handles valuation, while the tax commissioner handles the bill itself. The county's forms and applications page carries a Tax Commissioner Forms link. The assessor's number is (229) 723-3088. For anything else, the county administration building at 204 Court Square in Blakely answers at (229) 723-4304 on weekdays, closing for lunch at noon and reopening at 1:00 p.m. until 5:00 p.m.

Parcel records are on qPublic under the Early County listing. Payment questions, homestead applications and bill copies go to the commissioner, and appeals and appraised value questions go to the assessor.

  • Appraised value, property record or appeal: the assessor.
  • Bill copy, payment or homestead form: the tax commissioner.
  • Unsure where a form belongs: the administration office in Blakely.

sections.h2: Early County housing and market context
sections.html:
Blakely is the seat. Damascus, Jakin and Arlington are also cities, and Early shares Arlington with Calhoun County. Peanut farming drives much of the local income.

A typical owned home is worth $131,300 among 4,993 housing units, and only 12 building permits were issued in 2025, so new construction barely registers. With few new homes competing, a house with clean paperwork and no open tax issues stands out.

The county website also lists a code enforcement page and a code of ordinances on Municode. If your house has sat vacant, look at both, since clearing any open issue first gives a buyer fewer reasons to hesitate.

Appraisers may turn up at your parcel in any month. The county's standing notice cites O.C.G.A. 48-5-264.1 and names the triggers: a return, an appeal, a site improvement permit, a homestead or conservation use application, or a routine review. Keep permit paperwork for any addition you built, since building, electrical and manufactured home permits all reach the county. Staff collect only necessary details and photographs, and they leave a business card at an empty house. A visitor should show photo ID and arrive in a marked vehicle, and a call to the assessor settles any doubt.

Older owners can claim additional exemptions beyond the regular homestead one, with April 1 as the last day to apply. The law behind each exemption controls eligibility.

A redesigned Notice of Assessment under SB 566 lists exemptions and credits, estimates tax savings, names an appeal contact, spells out fair market value and says a homestead application may still be filed inside the 45-day appeal window. It also asks owners who are ineligible for a homestead exemption to say so before the window closes, because the tax and a 50 percent penalty stay with the property.

An owner who disputes a value writes to the Early County Assessor within 45 days of the notice's mailing date. The statewide appeal form lets you challenge taxability, value, uniformity or a refused exemption, and you choose a Board of Equalization, a hearing officer or an arbitrator on it.

Nobody at the state level can overrule the local decision makers on one parcel's value, whether that is the assessors, a Board of Equalization, a hearing officer, an arbitrator or Superior Court. Assessed value is 40 percent of fair market value, and the homestead exemption comes off that assessed figure before the millage rate applies.

The 2026 HOME Act ends the local opt-out from the HB 581 floating homestead exemption. The statewide version takes effect January 1, 2027 with 2026 values as its baseline, so a 2026 value carries weight beyond one tax year.

A homestead claim requires title and residence on January 1. File with the tax commissioner, or with the assessor in counties that delegate it, by the April 1 return deadline or during the 45-day appeal window. Before filing, do the following:

  • Save the notice and mark its mailing date.
  • Photograph defects and collect repair bids that support a lower value.
  • Request the property record card from the assessor and compare its square footage and condition notes with the house.
  • Ask which local exemptions Early County adds to the state's $2,000 standard exemption.

Early is thinly settled, with about 21 residents per square mile across 512.6 square miles of land. The estimated 10,455 residents in mid-2025 are 3.7 percent fewer than the 2020 base, and older adults make up 22.6 percent of the total, which makes the age-based exemptions especially relevant.

An heir or older owner preparing to sell should look for unpaid tax and budget for repairs.

Georgia charges the full year to whoever owned the parcel on January 1 and gives nothing back for a later sale. Most counties allow 60 days to pay with a normal due date of December 20, though local dates vary. The Early County tax commissioner can tell you the billing date and your parcel's balance.

Before signing a sale contract, ask the commissioner for a payoff number and whether any earlier years are still open. Liens issued by the commissioner are dealt with through that office. Filed liens appear on the clerk's general execution docket, so the clerk's index is worth a look as well.

Some Early County owners choose a no-repair cash sale for a house with a worn roof, tenants or back taxes, since the buyer absorbs the repairs and the balance is paid from proceeds.

Gather your latest notice of assessment, any permit paperwork for additions, and the homestead approval if you have one. Print the parcel record from qPublic so you can mark errors in square footage or condition.

When you call the assessor at (229) 723-3088, ask for the property record card and whether any exemption on file will end with the sale. When you call the commissioner, ask for the payoff in writing. Give both to the closing attorney so the settlement statement is correct the first time.

If the house is in an estate, ask the assessor which documents are needed before the owner of record can change. Record updates take time, and a payoff letter or homestead change may be held up until the file is complete. Starting that step before you list keeps the closing date from slipping.

Finally, if a mobile or manufactured home sits on the lot, confirm with the commissioner whether it has its own account, and settle it in the same visit as the land.

faqs.q: Which office sets values in Early County?
faqs.a: The Early County Assessor, reachable at (229) 723-3088, sets values and takes appeals. The tax commissioner bills and collects.

faqs.q: May Early County appraisers drop by unannounced?
faqs.a: Yes. A standing county notice allows visits all year for returns, appeals, permits, exemption applications or routine review. Staff show photo ID, use a marked vehicle and leave a card at an empty house.

faqs.q: What is the filing window for an Early County assessment appeal?
faqs.a: Forty-five days from the notice's mailing date. Write to the assessor and name your route: Board of Equalization, hearing officer or arbitrator.

faqs.q: What is the deadline for an Early County homestead exemption?
faqs.a: April 1 for the current year, or the 45-day appeal window after a notice. You must have owned and lived in the house on January 1.

faqs.q: If I sell in spring, is the Early County tax bill still mine?
faqs.a: Yes. The January 1 owner is responsible for the year, and Georgia gives no partial-year refund. Get the balance from the tax commissioner and settle it at closing.
